title: Gamaredon Group
summary: The Gamaredon Group, also reported as Primitive Bear, Shuckworm and Aqua Blizzard, is an espionage cluster whose activity concentrates on Ukrainian government, military and civil targets. Ukrainian authorities have publicly linked the activity to Russian security services, a claim repeated by several vendors, while other researchers describe the nexus as assessed rather than proven. Tradecraft in public reporting includes high-volume spear-phishing sent from compromised mailboxes, very short development cycles with frequent recompilation, and use of legitimate online services for command and control. The group is also known for aggressive self-propagation through removable media, network shares and documents. Detection therefore depends more on email anomaly rules, shared-drive monitoring and behavioural analytics than on stable file signatures, because the binaries change constantly. Attribution statements should always be quoted together with the source that makes them.

beginner.definition: The Gamaredon Group is a name for attackers who mainly target Ukraine. Public reports describe them as fast and noisy compared with other spying groups. They send many emails and change their tools often, so older virus signatures stop working quickly. Ukrainian officials have said the group is linked to Russian security services, and several vendors report the same assessment.
beginner.whyItMatters: Fast-changing malware defeats the idea that one antivirus scan is enough. This group floods mailboxes and reuses stolen accounts, so messages arrive from real colleagues you already trust. It also spreads across shared drives and memory sticks inside an office. If you work with Ukrainian partners or in a region under this kind of pressure, your detection must focus on behaviour rather than file names. Slow reporting makes the spread much worse.
howItWorks: The group takes over email accounts, then sends lures to everyone in the address book.
Messages arrive from real contacts, so readers trust them and open the attachments.
Opening the file runs a script that copies itself to shared folders and memory sticks.
That script connects to public online services, which hides the real control server.
The group rebuilds its files often, so signature-based tools quickly lose track of them.
Operators collect documents and credentials, then repeat the cycle with newly stolen accounts.
beginner.example: Imagine a rumour that spreads through an office by photocopying. Each person copies the note and puts a copy in every colleague's tray. The wording changes slightly each time, so nobody recognises it as the same note. That is how this group spreads. The changed wording is a recompiled file, and the trays are shared drives, memory sticks and mailboxes.
takeaways: Attacks that arrive from a colleague's real account are hard to spot.
Behaviour-based detection beats relying on file signatures alone.
Limit removable media and review who can write to shared folders.

objectives: Describe the targets and regional focus reported for the Gamaredon Group.
Explain why frequent recompilation defeats signature-based detection.
Identify self-propagation paths through shared folders and removable media.
Explain how compromised accounts are used to send further lures.
State attribution carefully and name the sources that make the claim.
